extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political theory and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for designing and judging mixed (composed) governments — including the roles of senate/assemblies, bicameralism, separation of powers, judicial composition, and institutional checks to preserve liberty and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate as counsellors, not commanders
rubrics_metrics.description: "The office of the senate is not to be commanders, but counsellors of the people; and that which is proper for counsellors is first to debate, and afterwards to give advice in the business whereon they have debated; whence the decrees of the senate are never laws..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The senate's proper function is deliberation and mature advice to be proposed to the people, not to unilaterally command or make laws. Anti-pattern: treating senatorial decrees as binding laws or as executive commands. Implementation notes: frame deliberations so they are 'maturely' formed before proposal to the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate as discernment (weighing reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: "To debate is to discern, or put a difference between things, that, being alike, are not the same; or it is separating and weighing this reason against that..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality deliberation must separate and weigh competing reasons; evaluation of a deliberative body should examine whether it genuinely distinguishes and balances reasons rather than merely splitting parties or issuing pronouncements. Anti-pattern: nominal debate that amounts to factional expression rather than reasoned weighing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bicameral division to produce wise and equal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: "...to establish a method of enacting laws that must of necessity be wise and equal, the people ... agreed upon that division of the legislative power into two houses, the house of representatives and the senate..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dividing legislative power into two chambers is prescribed to promote wisdom and equality in lawmaking. Assess designs by whether the bicameral structure meaningfully checks rush, faction, or concentrated interests and produces considered legislation. Historical example: U.S. division into representatives and senate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative assembly must reflect the whole intelligence of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: "...this council is to consist of such a representative as may be equal, and so constituted as it can never contradict any other intellect than that of the whole people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and constitution of representative bodies should aim to aggregate the general intelligence and interests of the polity so decisions cannot be dominated by a subset. Evaluation should consider representativeness, selection rules, and protections against a single class's capture. Anti-pattern: councils whose composition enables them to 'put out their light' (exclude other intellects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed/composed government combining monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "The wisest legislators... contrived another that partakes of them all, consisting of a prince, lords and commons ... every one of these members would be a check upon the other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-proportioned mixture of monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy provides mutual checks and greater durability. Assess constitutions by the balance among the three elements and by whether each estate/check is able to restrain abuses by the others. Examples: Sparta (Lycurgus) praised for longevity; Athens (Solon) shown as less stable when lacking a mixed balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers into legislative, executive, and judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: "In every government there are three sorts of power; the legislative, the executive ... and the executive in regard to things that depend on the civil law."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional liberty requires separating lawmaking, execution, and judging. Evaluation criterion: powers should be allocated so that no single person or body can both make, execute, and judge the same laws. Anti-patterns: unification of powers leading to arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: No liberty when legislative and executive powers are united
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine legislative and executive authority undermines liberty because the same actor can enact tyrannical laws and immediately execute them. Use examples (Turkey, some Italian republics) as warnings: where powers are united, subjects face arbitrary control. Evaluation should test formal and effective separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary must be distinct from other powers and composed from the people (not a standing senate)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judicary power ought not to be given to a standing senate; it should be exercised by persons taken from the body of the people ... in order to erect a tribunal that should last only as long as necessity requires."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer temporarily constituted or popularly drawn judicial tribunals over permanent, closed, elite tribunals for certain functions; this reduces concentration of judicial power. Evaluation: check whether judicial selection and tenure avoid creating an entrenched judicial oligarchy. Historical models: Athens' temporary juries; contrast with permanent senatorial courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges should be peers of the accused
rubrics_metrics.description: "The judges ought likewise to be in the same station as the accused, or, in other words, his peers, to the end that he may not imagine he is fallen into the hands of persons inclined to treat him with rigour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure composition and status parity of judges (where appropriate) to foster confidence and avoid perceived bias. Evaluation: whether tribunals include peers or representatives of the accused's status and whether procedural safeguards mitigate unequal treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused's privilege to choose or except judges in serious accusations
rubrics_metrics.description: "In accusations of a deep or criminal nature, it is proper the person accused should have the privilege of choosing, in some measure, his judges? or, at least, he should have a right to except against so great a number, that the remaining part may be deemed his own choice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural protections in grave cases should allow the accused some role in judge selection or exclusion to ensure fairness. Evaluation: presence of mechanisms for challenge/recusal or limited selection rights in serious criminal trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgments must conform to the exact letter of the law (not private opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Though the tribunals ought not to be fixed, yet the judgments ought, and to such a degree as to be always conformable to the exact letter of the law. Were they to be the private opinion of the judge, people would then live in society without knowing exactly the obligations it lays them under."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law application should be predictable and bound to statutory/established law rather than idiosyncratic judicial views. Evaluation looks at rule-of-law fidelity, predictability of decisions, and constraints on judicial discretion. Anti-pattern: judges issuing decisions based on personal views that upset legal certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple institutional checks to harness elite wisdom while restraining passions
rubrics_metrics.description: "...arranging them all... together in one assembly, by the name of a senate; by separating them from all pretensions to the executive power; and by controlling in the legislature their ambition and avarice, by an assembly of representatives on one side, and by the executive authority on the other... the benefit of their wisdom, without fear of their passions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should incorporate elites' expertise (aristocracy) in bodies like a senate while constraining their capacity to dominate via separate executive and representative mechanisms. Evaluation: whether institutional ties (executive, representative house, peers) effectively check oligarchic ambition and prevent capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent faction and provide mechanisms to replace or reconstitute councils
rubrics_metrics.description: Text excerpt: "A single council fails not to crumble, that is, to be factious; there being no dividing of the cake... nor is there any other remedy, but to have another council to choose."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid permanent single-council decision-making without counter-institutions; provide mechanisms (additional councils, reconstitution, elections) to prevent entrenched factions and enable corrective choice. Evaluation: presence of alternation, replacement procedures, or representative mixes that prevent factional capture and collapse into intrigue or violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit or check magistrates' power via institutional intermediaries (e.g., ephori, mayors, constable)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Some have permitted the crown to be hereditary as to its ordinary course; but restrained the power, and instituted officers to impede the proceedings of kings, and to take care that the laws were not violated. Of this sort were the Ephori of Sparta, the Maires du Palais, and afterwards the condable of France..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement offices or institutions designed specifically to check principal magistrates (hereditary or elective). Evaluation: whether checks (oversight officers, councils, tribunals) are empowered and effective at restraining executive/princely abuse without themselves becoming oligarchic.
